source.title: Understanding polysemanticity in neural networks through coding theory

record.file_problem: none; the full paper and supplementary material are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study uses an automated interpretability method associated with single-neuron explanations to evaluate explanations of random projections, but does not test the neuron-pole job shares or the claims about neuron explanations in the listed versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports GPT-2 XL eigenspectrum measurements and explanation scores for random projections. These do not measure the share of neurons with one or two jobs, or the performance of explanations for neuron poles. Single-neuron explanation scores are described as data extracted from reference [6], so they are not recorded as this study's own results.
record.test_reason: The study applies the Bills et al. automated-explanation pipeline to random projections of GPT-2 XL activations and reports its own method's scores. Its single-neuron curve is data extracted from ref. [6], an original source. It never measures how many neurons have one or two jobs, re-examines the cat-and-car neuron, builds neuron attribution graphs, or newly scores neuron explanations. Its view that polysemanticity is the default is a general coding-theory argument, not a measurement on any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors also conclude that the eigenspectrum of the activation covariance reveals a code's redundancy and error-correction capacity. Higher dropout gives faster-decaying eigenspectra, smoother random projections and more input variance explained. They argue that polysemantic or superposition codes are the efficient default.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes activation eigenspectra and scores explanations of random projections; it does not conduct a neuron-pole audit or test explanations of neuron poles on held-out activations.
record.method_sensitivity: Explanation scores vary non-monotonically with GPT-2 XL network depth; random-projection and single-neuron scores show opposing patterns.

fits_no_version.finding: In a ResNet-VAE, higher dropout gives faster-decaying activation eigenspectra (power-law exponent near -1 at 20% dropout), smoother random projections, and more input variance explained by random projections.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Dropout regularization shifts learned codes toward more redundant, linearly decodable population codes (measured at the population level, not per neuron).

fits_no_version.finding: In GPT-2 XL, the eigenspectrum power-law exponent stays above -1 across depth. Random-projection explanation scores are high in the layers where single-neuron scores (from [6]) are low.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Random-projection explanations may complement single-neuron explanations across layers of GPT-2 XL.

record.code_released: not stated; the paper says code would be made public after publication but gives no URL.
record.problems: The language-model analysis is on GPT-2 XL only. Figure 7b does not state numerical explanation-score values in the text, and the single-neuron comparison is extracted from another work. The study does not assess neuron-pole job shares.
record.rows_left_out: No rows for the eigenspectrum measurements: they characterize activation-code structure but do not measure neuron-pole job shares or any listed version's outcome. No row for the single-neuron score curve, which the text identifies as data extracted from reference [6].

untested.parts: Qwen3-32B neuron-pole job shares (about 90% one job, 7% two, 2–4% unknown).
Job shares in other dense and mixture-of-experts models and at large scale.
Reinterpretation of the InceptionV1 cat-and-car neuron as pose / recursive generalization.

Share of interpretable neurons as a function of tools, architecture and regularization. Dropout is varied, but only eigenspectrum decay and random-projection smoothness are measured, not neuron interpretability.
Neuron-based attribution graphs and reconstruction error.
Whether explanations fitted to activating examples fail to predict firing.
Share of neurons with good simulation scores. The single-neuron scores shown are taken from the original source [6], not re-measured.

missing.what: Eigenspectrum power-law exponents for GPT-2 XL across depth (Fig. 7a) and for the ResNet-VAE under varied dropout (Figs. 3, 5, 6). These bear on no version but matter as context for the regularization part of V4.

record.verdict_notes: The text asserts single-neuron methods work only for a 'small fraction' of neurons. That is an argument and a citation of Bills et al., not a new measurement, so it is not treated as a V7 or anti-V1 result. The text is a preprint, and code is in supplementary material only.

versions.untested_parts: The Qwen3-32B neuron-pole job shares and explanation test on held-out activations.
Job shares across models, model sizes, dense and mixture-of-experts architectures, and scales up to trillions of parameters.
The InceptionV1 cat-and-car neuron and the proposed pose / recursive-generalization interpretation.
The proposed causes of messy neurons and the estimates of interpretable-neuron shares in InceptionV1-sized vision models.
Attribution graphs built from a large model's own neurons and their reconstruction error.
Whether explanations that fit activating examples fail to predict where the neuron fires.
The share of neurons receiving good automated scores when neuron explanations are simulated on new text.

rows.subject: GPT-2 XL
rows.operation_detail: Scored explanations of random projections by simulating their activations on held-out text.
rows.measure: Explanation score: correlation between expected and real output.
rows.baseline: Single-neuron explanation scores from reference [6] are shown as a comparison; exact values not stated.
rows.value: figure only; the text says random-projection scores have the inverse depth pattern to single-neuron scores and perform well in layers where the single-neuron method performs poorly.
rows.uncertainty: 95% confidence intervals are indicated in Figure 7b; values not stated.
rows.note: The study's own explanation-score evaluation is for random projections, not neuron explanations. The single-neuron comparison is identified as data extracted from reference [6].
rows.check: This row is the study's own method (random-projection explanations) compared with a single-neuron curve copied from Bills et al. [6]. It is not a measurement of neuron explanation quality. Values are figure-only. Explanations come from GPT-4 and simulation from text-davinci-003. The 'observed' state has no version to attach to, so it should be cannot_determine.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
